# What else can a bot trade?

*You'll need the fair value (chapter 3), why making earns (chapter 4), informed traders (chapter 5), what a position
costs (chapter 6), levels and jumps (chapter 7), fill models (chapter 10), and held-out days (chapter 11).*

## The story

In Prosperity 2, a team called Linear Utility went into round 4 in second place. The round added a coconut coupon, a
call option on coconuts with a strike of 10,000 and 250 days to expiry. They priced it with Black–Scholes, saw its
implied volatility swing around 16%, and traded the swings, as they had traded a basket the round before. To bet on the
volatility alone they needed to hedge the coupon's exposure to coconuts. They couldn't fully: the coupon's delta was
about 0.53, so 600 coupons, their limit, moved like about 318 coconuts, and they were allowed 300. About 18 deltas were
left over, and they chose to hold them: "holding delta with vega was still positive ev (but higher var)"
[(`references/prosperity2-linear-utility/README.md:162-166`)]{.src}.

The variance came. They "got unlucky and lost money from our delta exposure", made only 145 thousand in the round, in that
edition's seashells, and fell to 26th. Their verdict: "we were already second place and thus should've went for lower var to try and keep the lead"
[(`references/prosperity2-linear-utility/README.md:168-170`)]{.src}.

What failed was a piece of exposure they knew about and kept. Market making earns a little on every trade and holds
as little as it can; every strategy in this chapter decides to hold a position, because something it measures says the
price will come to it. The question each time is what the bot is really betting on.

## The idea

### A target instead of a quote

The template's market maker (chapter 4) has no view: it wants a position of zero and leans on its quotes to get back
there. Each of the template's *target modes* replaces that zero with a number. Some rule outside the book says "hold +60 now", and the bot's execution moves toward it, normally at once, crossing
the spread up to `clear_edge` from fair. With `cross_excess` set, it crosses only for the part of the gap beyond that
many lots and works the rest passively (only Hydrogel sets it, at 25)
[(`python/bots/template.py`, `clear`; `IDEAS.md`, "Passive-first execution toward a target")]{.src}. Market making can
carry on around the target with whatever room is left.

The table lists the modes, what each bets on, and what Prosperity data said.

| Mode | Bets that | Measured on | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `level` | a price returns to a known level | P4 Hydrogel, Velvetfruit | kept |
| `basket` | a basket's spread against its legs returns to its usual value | P3 and P2 baskets | kept, taking only; hedging dropped here |
| `smile` | an option is mispriced against its underlying | P3 and P2 options | kept, take-only; the hedge dropped here |
| `follow` | an option carries its underlying's level bet, with more room | P4 options | kept |
| `copy` | one named trader knows where the price is going | P3's Olivia, P4's Marks | kept for Olivia; the Marks dropped here |
| `jump` | a jump in the price snaps straight back | P4 round 5 | kept, off by default |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
Six modes. Level bets that a price returns to a known level, and is kept. Basket bets that a basket's spread against
its legs returns to its usual value, and is kept for taking only. Smile bets that an option is mispriced against its underlying, and is kept for taking only, without the hedge. Follow
lets an option carry its underlying's level bet, and is kept. Copy follows one named trader who knows where the price is going, kept for
Olivia only. Jump bets that a jump snaps straight back, kept but off by default.
:::

Every row is a Prosperity result, so every verdict is a prior to re-test on the Arena's data, and "dropped here" means
dropped on Prosperity's days, nothing more [(`IDEAS.md`, rows by mode, below)]{.src}.

### Levels

Chapter 7 introduced the level. In brief: on Prosperity 4's Hydrogel and Velvetfruit each day's mean sat close to
the others': Hydrogel's between 9,989 and 10,003 credits, against standard deviations of 25 to 38 within a day
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Trading toward a known level")]{.src}. So the template holds its full limit short once the price is more
than `level_band` above `level`, and long once it is as far below. Choosing the level and settings on three days and
scoring the fourth made 149.9 thousand credits on Hydrogel and 98.9 thousand on Velvetfruit over the four held-out
days. Taking the level from the day so far instead of from the other days cost about a third: 184.9 thousand against
280.2 with the same settings [(`data/level_mode.csv`, from `experiments.day.p4_level_template`)]{.src}. A level bet is only as good as the level.

### Baskets and their spread

A *basket* is a product whose value is a fixed bundle of others. Prosperity 3's `PICNIC_BASKET1` contained 6 Croissants,
3 Jams and 1 Djembes; it traded on its own book, next to the books of its three legs. The quantity to watch is the
*spread*, the template's `basket` mode's signal:

::: {.eq speak="the basket's spread is the basket's price less the weighted sum of its legs' prices"}
$$\text{spread} = \text{basket} - \sum_i w_i \times \text{leg}_i$$
:::

with each [$w_i$]{speak="w i"} the number of units of leg i in the basket and every price a wall mid (`python/bots/template.py`,
`basket_target`). The template then treats the spread as a level: short the basket when the spread is far above its
usual value, long when far below.

The figure below (@fig-basket) shows why that works on Prosperity 3. Over a day the basket and its legs wander together by hundreds of
credits, while their difference swings around a premium and keeps returning to it within the day. But the premium moves between days: a mean of 70, then 44, then 32, against
swings of 79 to 89 [(`data/basket_days.csv`)]{.src}.

![Top: Prosperity 3's `PICNIC_BASKET1` and its six Croissants, three Jams and one Djembes over day 0 of round 2. Bottom:
their difference over the round's three days, each day's mean in black, and the template's bands at its level 49 plus
and minus 84, dashed. Data: `data/basket_spread.csv`, from the days themselves.](../figures/g11_basket_spread.png){#fig-basket
fig-alt="Top: the basket and the weighted legs both fall from about 59,300 to 58,700 credits over one day, close together. Bottom: the spread swings between minus 185 and plus 237, around daily means of 70, 44 and 32 credits, crossing the template's bands at 133 and minus 35 a few times a day."}

With each day's level and band taken from the other
two days, the baskets made 70.7 thousand credits over Prosperity 3's round 2, against 20.2 thousand for plain market
making on the same products; chosen on all three days, 139.2. On Prosperity 2's gift basket, 294.3 thousand held out
against 20.3 [(`IDEAS.md`, "Trading a basket's spread"; re-run with `experiments.day.baskets`)]{.src}.

First, *hedging with the legs never won*. The spread closed mostly by the basket moving, so the legs only
added costs: 122.2 and 122.4
thousand with half and with a full hedge, against 139.2 without. Second, the baskets only take. Their prices jump several
ticks at once, so resting quotes on them were picked off: −321 thousand credits on Prosperity 3 under `--resting`
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Trading a basket's spread")]{.src}. Baskets nobody announced, found by search on Prosperity 4's round 5, didn't hold on held-out days
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Residual baskets beyond an identity")]{.src}.

### Options in a page

A *call option* is the right, not the obligation, to buy an underlying at a fixed *strike* price on a fixed day. If
the underlying ends above the strike, the call pays the difference; otherwise nothing. So its value today depends on
how likely the underlying is to end above the strike, and by how much, which depends on how much the underlying moves:
its *volatility*.

Black–Scholes turns that into a price. It assumes the underlying's log price wanders like a random walk with a fixed
volatility, [$\sigma$]{speak="sigma"}, and asks what a portfolio that copies the option's payoff would cost. The answer is the underlying's
price times one normal probability less the strike times another: no forecast of direction enters it, only the price,
the strike, the time left and the volatility. Run it backwards and a market price gives an *implied volatility*: the volatility at which Black–Scholes reproduces the price. It is the market's price restated in units that compare across strikes.

If the model were exactly right, every strike would show the same implied volatility. In Prosperity 3 they don't: plotted against *moneyness*, the log of the strike over the price scaled by the square root of the time left, the
implied vols trace a curve, the *smile*. The figure below (@fig-voucher-smile) shows Prosperity 3's volcanic rock vouchers on all five of their distinct days. One parabola fits them all; fitted on four days, it misses the fifth by
under one point of volatility [(`data/voucher_smile_fit.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "Options: trading implied-volatility deviations from a fitted smile, delta hedging")]{.src}.

![Implied volatility of Prosperity 3's five volcanic rock vouchers against moneyness, on the five distinct days with
vouchers, and the parabola fitted to all of them. Data: `data/voucher_smile.csv`, from `experiments.day.p3_smile`'s
points.](../figures/g12_voucher_smile.png){#fig-voucher-smile
fig-alt="Points for five strikes lie along one U-shaped curve, from about 28 percent volatility for strikes far below the rock's price, down to about 15 percent at the money, and up to about 27 percent for strikes far above it."}

The last idea is *delta*: how many units of the underlying the option moves like. Under Black–Scholes, with no
interest,

::: {.eq speak="an option's delta is the normal curve's area up to d one, where d one is the log of the price over the strike, plus half the variance to expiry, all over the volatility times the square root of the time left"}
$$\Delta = N(d_1), \qquad d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + \sigma^2 T / 2}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}$$
:::

with S the underlying's price, K the strike, T the time to expiry in years and N the normal distribution's cumulative
probability [(`python/bots/template.py`, `call_delta`; DTU's helpers, `references/prosperity4-dtu-quant-lab/round_3/algorithmic/trader.py:426-430`)]{.src}. Delta runs from near 0 far out of the
money to near 1 deep in it, as Harris describes in words (*Trading and Exchanges*, §17.3.1.3, PDF p. 368). A trader
who wants to bet on volatility alone holds minus delta units of the underlying per option: that is the hedge Linear
Utility couldn't complete.

### What paid on Prosperity's options

The template's `smile` mode prices each voucher at Black–Scholes on the fitted smile, plus the voucher's usual offset
from it, and takes any book order that strays from that fair. On the two strikes near the money it made 528.8 thousand
credits over the five days, every day positive, the same under every fill model. The controls took that apart. One flat volatility for every strike did as well (567.0 thousand with quotes, against 559.4 with the smile), and
no option model at all lost 76.4 thousand. The controls suggest the edge was pricing each voucher off the rock's latest price, and that the smile's shape added
nothing. The delta hedge cost 49.9 to 256.4 thousand in every variant, and quotes left resting on the vouchers lost 0.6 to 2.6 million (0.6 to 1.5 million unhedged) [(`IDEAS.md`, "Options: trading implied-volatility deviations from a fitted smile, delta hedging"; re-run with `experiments.day.p3_smile --engine rust`)]{.src}.

Prosperity 4's vouchers had a flat volatility within each day, so each was the underlying at a fixed delta; the
template's `follow` mode lets them carry the underlying's level bet with more room: 768 thousand credits held out over four days, Velvetfruit and its vouchers together (the vouchers
alone 661 thousand) [(`IDEAS.md`, "What the P4 vouchers are")]{.src}. On
Prosperity 2's coupon, Linear Utility's own product, the residual drifted instead of reverting, and `smile` paid only
with an offset averaged over 5,000 ticks (chapter 7). And CMU Physics' fitted smile stopped fitting on the day they were scored; a short rolling window of implied vol took
their backtest from about 80 thousand to 200 thousand a day, *their claim* [(`references/online-snapshots/chrispyroberts_imc-prosperity-3.README.md:236`)]{.src}. On three
markets, the smile was the least useful part of the textbook.

### Copying the informed, and fading jumps

Two modes read something other than prices. The `copy` mode follows named traders (chapter 5's Olivia): each of her trades sets
the target to the limit her way. On top of plain market making it took Prosperity 3's Croissants from 1.4 to 2.1
thousand credits a day to 13.5 to 25.9 thousand. Choosing whom to follow is the hard part. Picking names by their mean
move on two days and trading them on the third lost 399.5 thousand; picking only names that were right on 80% of
trades on each training day chose Olivia alone, and made 54.1 thousand held out, over Prosperity 3's round 5. The hit-rate rule was written after the mean rule
failed, so it is not a clean test [(`IDEAS.md`, "Following informed counterparties")]{.src}.

The `jump` mode fades jumps. On one product-day of Prosperity 4, `ROBOT_DISHES`' wall mid sat on multiples of 100 and stepped by
100, and 87% of its 741 jumps were followed by a move the other way. Holding the limit against each jump made 958.8 thousand
credits over round 5's three days against 457.8 for plain market making, 429.1 thousand of it on that one product-day.
A gate makes it safe to switch on everywhere: it trades only once most of the day's jumps have reversed; without it,
fading every jump lost 184.1 thousand on one day. All of these settings were chosen on these three
days [(`IDEAS.md`, "Fading jumps that snap back")]{.src}.

### Edges a replay can't value, and edges that aren't allowed

Some edges a replay can't test. In Prosperity 4's round 1, one side of the book was empty on about 7.6%
of ticks, and Baguette Fromage found that a hidden taker would sometimes lift a quote about 100 from fair on that
side: an expected 18.6 thousand credits a day on Osmium, *their claim*
[(`references/prosperity4-baguette-fromage/README.md:352-365`)]{.src}. DU reports an admin saying the generator removed 20% of the bots' orders at random
[(`references/prosperity4-du-trading/README.md:77`)]{.src}. Our engine can't value it at
all: no recorded trade ever printed outside the visible book, so a far quote fills nothing in any mode
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Quoting far away when one side of the book is empty")]{.src}.

And some edges are leaks. Hunting for how another team made 1.2 million in one round, Linear Utility regressed that
year's prices on the *previous* year's public data: last year's diving gear, times about 3, predicted this year's
roses with an R-squared of 0.99, and last year's coconuts predicted this year's with a beta of 1.25. They called it "fair
game", since the data was public, and spent the last round trading on known future prices
[(`references/prosperity2-linear-utility/README.md:176-182`)]{.src}. A year later the bots behaved like the previous
year's to over 95%, so teams hard-coded trades at known timestamps. Frankfurt Hedgehogs reported it after round 2;
IMC fixed the bots, banned hard-coding and re-ran the first two rounds
[(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:967-976`)]{.src}. CMU Physics, 771st when round 1 was first ranked (other teams had hard-coded the live day from the website's sample
data, and a Squid Ink spike went against them), were 9th once it was re-run, where the spike went their way: "We got
lucky" [(`references/online-snapshots/chrispyroberts_imc-prosperity-3.README.md:70-72`)]{.src}.

A leak is the purest edge, and the one most likely to be taken away or to count as cheating; chapter 9 says how the
repo keeps such a bot from being uploaded by accident.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
A target mode is a forecaster whose output is a position rather than a price. The basket's spread is the residual of a linear model whose weights are given, and trading it is trading the
residual's mean reversion, as with cointegration. Implied volatility is a reparametrisation, like logits for
probabilities: a monotone transform that makes prices across strikes comparable, so a smile is a calibration curve.
Where the analogy breaks: in ML a better-fitting model is usually the better one. Here the better fit (the smile)
added nothing over a flat volatility, and the "complete" model, with the hedge, lost money.
:::
